text: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree and return its root.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — invert here means mirror the tree left to right. At every node, the left child and the right child trade places, and that happens all the way down, not just at the root. Is that right?

Good. Then let me say what a mirror means in terms I can test. If I read the tree left to right — that's an inorder walk — mirroring should give me the same values back in the opposite order. So inorder of the inverted tree is the reverse of inorder of the original. I want to be careful not to over-claim, though: the same is not true for preorder. Preorder always puts the root first, and reversing would put it last, so the two only agree on a tree of zero or one nodes. Inorder works because it's the only one of the three where the node sits between its two subtrees.
A couple more. Should I build a new tree, or change this one? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Changing it in place is fine. Up to one hundred nodes. The root can be null.

Let me run through the example: four, two, seven, one, three, six, nine. Root four, left two with children one and three, right seven with children six and nine. After mirroring, seven moves to the left of the root and two to the right, and inside each, the pairs swap too: seven's children become nine then six, and two's become three then one. So level order reads four, seven, two, nine, six, three, one. That matches. And my check holds: inorder goes from one, two, three, four, six, seven, nine to the exact reverse.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to read the tree level by level, reverse each level's values, and write them back. That only moves values, never shape — on a lopsided tree like one, null, two, the lone child stays on the right, so it's simply wrong, and it builds extra arrays too. This problem reminds me of the standard depth-first recursion on a tree. The mirror of a tree is: mirror the left subtree, mirror the right subtree, then swap the two child pointers. The definition is recursive, so the code can be too.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is empty, return empty. Two: mirror the left subtree and the right subtree. Three: swap the two child pointers and return the node. Here, I'm using the return value to keep track of the subtree root; since I mutate in place, it's always the node I was handed. One thing worth flagging — I swap the child pointers, not the values. Swapping values moves numbers while the shape stays the same, which is wrong whenever the two sides have different shapes, and it skips any node with only one child. Swapping pointers moves the whole subtree, shape and all. There's a trade-off here: an explicit queue avoids recursion depth, but it's more lines, and with a hundred nodes recursion is safe. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Null returns null; otherwise I invert both subtrees, assign them back, swap the two pointers, and return the root. One thing worth flagging — I recurse first and swap after, so the swaps happen on the way back up, in postorder: the deepest nodes first, the root last. That's not a requirement. Swapping first and then recursing is also correct, because the swap at a node and the mirroring inside its subtrees touch different pointers. What matters is that every node gets swapped exactly once, and that I swap pointers rather than values. And a leaf still swaps two null pointers — a harmless no-op.

Let's dry-run the code on four, two, seven, one, three, six, nine, expected four, seven, two, nine, six, three, one. The row that matters is the last swap, at the root: by then both subtrees are already mirrored, so it moves two finished subtrees, not half-done ones. Before that, the leaves under two swap, then two, then the leaves under seven, then seven. That matches. Corner cases: an empty tree returns null. A single node swaps two nulls and comes back unchanged — it's its own mirror. One, two becomes one, null, two — exactly the case a value swap would skip, since there's no second value to pair with.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: exactly two n plus one calls, one per node plus one per empty link, since an n-node binary tree has exactly n plus one empty links. Constant work each. Space is O of h for the call stack, where h is the height, and I allocate nothing — no new nodes, no extra arrays. In the worst case the tree is one long chain, so h equals n; balanced, it's about log n. At a hundred nodes that's not a concern; on a very deep tree I'd switch to the queue version. Oh, one more thing — this is fully in place: same nodes, same returned root. The flip side is that the original tree is gone, so if a caller still needs it, I'd copy first and say so at the API boundary.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You turned mirror into a testable identity — inorder of the inverted tree is the reverse of the original — and held yourself to it by pointing out the same claim is false for preorder, with the reason. You separated what matters from what doesn't: swapping before or after the recursion is both fine, but swapping pointers instead of values isn't negotiable, and you named the one-child node that value swapping misses. And you closed on the in-place property precisely, including the cost of destroying the original. Good work.
